Notation

This table collects the notation used in the main text and the appendices. Each entry gives the meaning of a symbol. The same letter sometimes has a different meaning in a proof or experiment; these uses are listed separately. Block subscripts and fixed arguments are occasionally suppressed in proofs, so f,f^,R,R^,D,g,U,q,δ,δ∗,δU,εf,\widehat{f},R,\widehat{R},D,g,U,q,\delta,\delta^{*},\delta^{U},\varepsilon then denote the corresponding block quantities. The index jj denotes a coordinate within a block, a color class, or a single-agent answer, as stated. A hat denotes an implemented approximation or an estimate, not a different task.

Appendix A Further theory and examples

This appendix extends Sections 3–7 and uses their notation; the table on page Notation lists every symbol. All guarantees concern the specified objective FF, not requirements that its evaluation omits, and private work means computation without communication, not confidential data. Section A.1 works through small examples of the model. Section A.2 treats a uniform correction-error bound, characterizes the block error bound, gives an optimality certificate and proves the bound along a recorded run used in Section 8.1. Section A.3 proves the private-work horizon of Section 7. Sections A.4 and A.5 develop the learning theory summarized in Section 6, with its certificate and cost. The best-combination merge and its guarantees are stated in Section 5, with a conflict-greedy variant in Appendix E.9.

A.1. Examples

Why local improvement may not help.

A module can pass its isolated tests while returning a format that another module cannot read. An agent searching only with those tests has no reason to repair the format. We call the difference between what the local and global objectives reward an objective mismatch. More local search does not necessarily make this mismatch larger; it may simply solve the wrong local problem more accurately. Checking a proposal globally can reject it, but rejection alone does not tell the agent how to search better.

The following one-decision example isolates this issue. Let u=0u=0 mean retaining an incompatible output format and u=1u=1 mean repairing it. Let FF be the global objective and LL the local objective, both minimized:

(A.1) F⁡(u)=1−u,L⁡(u)=u,u∈{0,1}.F(u)=1-u,\qquad L(u)=u,\qquad u\in\{0,1\}.

Starting at zero, even an exact minimizer of LL keeps the incompatible format, whereas FF is minimized at one.

Verification therefore protects the current solution but does not resolve the cause of the failed search. To produce a useful proposal, the agent needs a different criterion for comparing its candidates, and the correction supplies it. At base u=0u=0, the local change from choosing one is +1+1, while the global change is −1-1. A correction of −2-2 to that candidate’s local change makes the corrected score prefer the repair, and the correction at the unchanged candidate is zero, as anchoring requires.

A two-block example.

Let x1,x2∈{0,1}x_{1},x_{2}\in\{0,1\} encode two decisions. Each local objective prefers zero, but the global objective prefers one and also penalizes disagreement:

(A.2) L1​(u)=L2​(u)=u,F⁡(x)=(1−x1)+(1−x2)+14​(x1−x2)2.\begin{gathered}L_{1}(u)=L_{2}(u)=u,\\ F(x)=(1-x_{1})+(1-x_{2})+\tfrac{1}{4}(x_{1}-x_{2})^{2}.\end{gathered}

Starting from x=(0,0)x=(0,0), the loss is 2. Changing either block to one lowers it to 1.251.25, although its local objective rises by 1. Thus the exact anchored correction at that candidate is −1.75-1.75: adding it to the local change gives the true change −0.75-0.75. For either block, the corrected score of leaving it unchanged is zero.

Block-1 choice Local change Correction Sum
Keep u=0u=0 0 0 0
Choose u=1u=1 1 −1.75-1.75 −0.75-0.75

Section A.4 returns to it to show how objective evaluations reveal its unknown correction coefficients.

One update.

The two blocks share the disagreement factor, so they have different colors. With exact local minimization, both propose one, with singleton gain 0.750.75. Either color is best. Break the tie in favor of block 1: the next solution is (1,0)(1,0) and its loss is 1.251.25. At this new base, changing block 2 to one improves the loss by 1.251.25, and the next update reaches (1,1)(1,1) with loss zero. Notice that the conditional score changed when its neighboring block changed; a correction must be evaluated at the current base.

Changes that clash.

Two blocks that share a factor can each lower the loss alone and yet raise it together. On two binary blocks, let

F⁡(x)=(1−x1)+(1−x2)+3​x1​x2.F(x)=(1-x_{1})+(1-x_{2})+3x_{1}x_{2}.

From x=(0,0)x=(0,0), with loss 2, changing either block to one lowers the loss to 1, but changing both raises it to 3, like two robots that take the same shortcut and collide. The factor 3​x1​x23x_{1}x_{2} joins the two blocks, so they have different colors, and Algorithm 1 accepts only one of the two changes.

A single-block trap.

Even a perfect correction cannot resolve a task that violates Assumption 3. For example, on two binary blocks let F⁡(0,0)=1F(0,0)=1, F⁡(1,0)=F⁡(0,1)=2F(1,0)=F(0,1)=2, and F⁡(1,1)=0F(1,1)=0. At (0,0)(0,0), neither single-block change helps, so D1+D2=0D_{1}+D_{2}=0 while the global gap is 1. Joint search or acceptance of intermediate worsening is needed. The parameter μ\mu describes the task, rather than the agent or communication protocol.

A.2. Further convergence results

A uniform correction-error bound.

A bound on the correction error at every candidate,

(A.3) supu∈𝒳b|R^b​(u,x)−Rb​(u,x)|≤δb,\sup_{u\in\mathcal{X}_{b}}|\widehat{R}_{b}(u;x)-R_{b}(u;x)|\leq\delta_{b},

implies Assumption 1 with δb∗=δbU=δb\delta_{b}^{*}=\delta_{b}^{U}=\delta_{b}. Lemma 1 then gives

(A.4) 𝔼⁡[gb∣ℋ]≥qb​(H)​Db​(x)−(1+qb​(H))​δb,\mathbb{E}[g_{b}\mid\mathcal{H}]\geq q_{b}(H)D_{b}(x)-(1+q_{b}(H))\delta_{b},

and Theorem 2 holds with B=Bδ≔κ−1​∑b(1+qb​(H))​δbB=B_{\delta}\coloneqq\kappa^{-1}\sum_{b}(1+q_{b}(H))\delta_{b}. Such a bound must also hold for poor candidates that no reasonable search returns, so it can be far larger than the two-point constants; in routing it exceeds 10410^{4} (Appendix E.7). Lemma 1 and the first step of the proof of Theorem 2 hold epoch by epoch, conditionally on ℋ\mathcal{H}, so they remain valid when δb\delta_{b} changes between epochs:

(A.5) 𝔼⁡[F⁡(x)−F⁡(x+)∣ℋ]≥α​Δ​(x)−Bδ.\mathbb{E}[F(x)-F(x^{+})\mid\mathcal{H}]\geq\alpha\Delta(x)-B_{\delta}.

The learning results of Sections A.4 and A.5 use them in this form.

A relative correction error.

If instead qb​(H)​δb∗+δbU≤ζ​qb​(H)​Db​(x)q_{b}(H)\delta_{b}^{*}+\delta_{b}^{U}\leq\zeta q_{b}(H)D_{b}(x) for a fixed ζ<1\zeta<1 at every epoch, the proof of Theorem 2 gives the contraction factor 1−(1−ζ)​μ​q​(H)/κ1-(1-\zeta)\mu q(H)/\kappa and no floor. This relative certificate is useful analytically but is not automatically observable: DbD_{b} is usually unknown.

How restrictive is the block error bound?

On a finite domain, existence of some positive constant has a simple characterization. The size of that constant is a separate question: it may be arbitrarily small. The following observation also explains when a computable stopping certificate is available.

Proposition A.1 (Block geometry and an optimality certificate).

On the full finite product domain, a constant μ∈(0,1]\mu\in(0,1] satisfying (12) exists if and only if every point with Db​(x)=0D_{b}(x)=0 for all bb is globally optimal. When this local-to-global property holds and there are suboptimal points, one valid choice is

(A.6) μfin≔min{1,minx:Δ⁡(x)>0∑bDb​(x)Δ⁡(x)}.\mu_{\rm fin}\coloneqq\min\left\{1,\min_{x:\Delta(x)>0}\frac{\sum_{b}D_{b}(x)}{\Delta(x)}\right\}.

If every point is optimal, take μfin=1\mu_{\rm fin}=1. Moreover, at any base where a known μ>0\mu>0 satisfies (12), exact block improvements give

(A.7) Δ⁡(x)​≤(12)​1μ​∑bDb​(x).\Delta(x)\overset{\eqref{eq:eb}}{\leq}\frac{1}{\mu}\sum_{b}D_{b}(x).

More generally, suppose certified bounds δb\delta_{b} satisfy (A.3) and computable lower bounds f¯b≤minu⁡f^b​(u,x)\underline{f}_{b}\leq\min_{u}\widehat{f}_{b}(u;x) are available. Then

(A.8) Δ⁡(x)​≤(12),(A.3),(3),(4)​1μ​∑b(δb−f¯b).\Delta(x)\overset{\eqref{eq:eb},\eqref{dev:eq:error},\eqref{eq:correction},\eqref{eq:surrogate}}{\leq}\frac{1}{\mu}\sum_{b}(\delta_{b}-\underline{f}_{b}).
Proof idea.

Finiteness turns strictly positive improvement ratios into a positive minimum. For certification, the error bound converts upper bounds on exact block improvements into an upper bound on the global gap.

Proof.

If (12) holds and all Db​(x)D_{b}(x) vanish, then Δ⁡(x)=0\Delta(x)=0. Conversely, the stated local-to-global property makes every ratio in (A.6) positive; the nonempty set of ratios is finite, so its minimum is positive. At a global optimum every DbD_{b} is zero, and hence the resulting constant satisfies (12) everywhere. For the approximate certificate, uniform error gives

(A.9) minu⁡fb​(u,x)​≥(A.3),(3),(4)​minu​f^b​(u,x)−δb≥f¯b−δb,Db​(x)​≤(11),(A.3),(3),(4)​δb−f¯b.\begin{gathered}\min_{u}f_{b}(u;x)\overset{\eqref{dev:eq:error},\eqref{eq:correction},\eqref{eq:surrogate}}{\geq}\min_{u}\widehat{f}_{b}(u;x)-\delta_{b}\geq\underline{f}_{b}-\delta_{b},\\ D_{b}(x)\overset{\eqref{eq:gap},\eqref{dev:eq:error},\eqref{eq:correction},\eqref{eq:surrogate}}{\leq}\delta_{b}-\underline{f}_{b}.\end{gathered}

Combining these bounds yields

Δ⁡(x)​≤(12)​1μ​∑bDb​(x)​≤(A.9)​1μ​∑b(δb−f¯b),\Delta(x)\overset{\eqref{eq:eb}}{\leq}\frac{1}{\mu}\sum_{b}D_{b}(x)\overset{\eqref{eq:stop-block}}{\leq}\frac{1}{\mu}\sum_{b}(\delta_{b}-\underline{f}_{b}),

which proves (A.8). The same bound holds with δb\delta_{b} replaced by a bound δb∗\delta_{b}^{*} on the error at a true block minimizer. ∎

Neither enumerating (A.6) nor solving all block subproblems is automatically cheap. Approximate proposals give lower bounds on available improvement, whereas stopping needs upper bounds. An exact block solve or a certified lower bound on each surrogate minimum supplies the missing direction. A known valid μ\mu is also required. Thus the generic local solver does not automatically provide a stopping test, but the theory does permit one when this additional information is available.

Local-to-global results in discrete convex analysis depend on the allowed neighborhood: coordinated subset moves or exchanges may be essential (Murota, 2003). Merely calling an objective discrete convex does not establish (12) for the fixed disjoint blocks used here.

A bound along a recorded run.

The argument of Lemma 1 also applies to a single realized epoch, with realized local progress in place of qb​(H)q_{b}(H) and realized two-point errors in place of δb∗,δbU\delta_{b}^{*},\delta_{b}^{U}.

Proposition A.2 (Bound along a recorded run).

Fix a realized epoch kk with base x=xkx=x^{k} and Δ⁡(x)>0\Delta(x)>0. Suppose that every returned block scores no worse than the current block, that is, f^b​(Ub,x)≤0\widehat{f}_{b}(U_{b};x)\leq 0. Write

εb​(u)≔f^b​(u,x)−fb​(u,x),D^b≔−minu⁡f^b​(u,x).\varepsilon_{b}(u)\coloneqq\widehat{f}_{b}(u;x)-f_{b}(u;x),\qquad\widehat{D}_{b}\coloneqq-\min_{u}\widehat{f}_{b}(u;x).

Let Qb≔−f^b(Ub;x)/D^b∈[0,1]Q_{b}\coloneqq-\widehat{f}_{b}(U_{b};x)/\widehat{D}_{b}\in[0,1] if D^b>0\widehat{D}_{b}>0 and Qb≔0Q_{b}\coloneqq 0 otherwise, and let eb∗≔|εb​(ub∗)|e^{*}_{b}\coloneqq|\varepsilon_{b}(u_{b}^{*})| for a true block minimizer ub∗u_{b}^{*} and ebU≔|εb​(Ub)|e^{U}_{b}\coloneqq|\varepsilon_{b}(U_{b})|. Then the merge of Algorithm 1 gives

(A.10) Δ⁡(x+)≤min⁡{Δ⁡(x),(1−αk)​Δ​(x)+Bk},\Delta(x^{+})\leq\min\{\Delta(x),\,(1-\alpha_{k})\Delta(x)+B_{k}\},

where

αk≔min⁡{1,∑bQb​Db​(x)κ​Δ​(x)},Bk≔1κ​∑b(Qb​eb∗+ebU).\alpha_{k}\coloneqq\min\Bigl\{1,\frac{\sum_{b}Q_{b}D_{b}(x)}{\kappa\Delta(x)}\Bigr\},\qquad B_{k}\coloneqq\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{b}(Q_{b}e^{*}_{b}+e^{U}_{b}).

Consequently, if every epoch with Δ⁡(xk)>0\Delta(x^{k})>0 satisfies these hypotheses, and with αk≔Bk≔0\alpha_{k}\coloneqq B_{k}\coloneqq 0 once Δ⁡(xk)=0\Delta(x^{k})=0, which then persists because the objective never increases, the sequence E0=Δ⁡(x0)E_{0}=\Delta(x^{0}), Ek+1=min⁡{Ek,(1−αk)​Ek+Bk}E_{k+1}=\min\{E_{k},(1-\alpha_{k})E_{k}+B_{k}\} satisfies Δ⁡(xk)≤Ek\Delta(x^{k})\leq E_{k} for every kk.

Proof.

If D^b>0\widehat{D}_{b}>0, then −D^b≤f^b​(ub∗,x)=−Db​(x)+εb​(ub∗)-\widehat{D}_{b}\leq\widehat{f}_{b}(u_{b}^{*};x)=-D_{b}(x)+\varepsilon_{b}(u_{b}^{*}), so −f^b​(Ub,x)=Qb​D^b≥Qb​(Db​(x)−eb∗)-\widehat{f}_{b}(U_{b};x)=Q_{b}\widehat{D}_{b}\geq Q_{b}(D_{b}(x)-e^{*}_{b}). Hence

gb≥−fb​(Ub,x)\displaystyle g_{b}\geq-f_{b}(U_{b};x) =−f^b​(Ub,x)+εb​(Ub)\displaystyle=-\widehat{f}_{b}(U_{b};x)+\varepsilon_{b}(U_{b})
≥Qb​Db​(x)−Qb​eb∗−ebU.\displaystyle\geq Q_{b}D_{b}(x)-Q_{b}e^{*}_{b}-e^{U}_{b}.

If D^b=0\widehat{D}_{b}=0, the right-hand side is −ebU≤0≤gb-e^{U}_{b}\leq 0\leq g_{b}. Summing over blocks and using (8), Δ⁡(x)−Δ⁡(x+)≥κ−1​∑bgb≥αk​Δ​(x)−Bk\Delta(x)-\Delta(x^{+})\geq\kappa^{-1}\sum_{b}g_{b}\geq\alpha_{k}\Delta(x)-B_{k}; capping αk\alpha_{k} at one only weakens this inequality, and Δ⁡(x+)≤Δ⁡(x)\Delta(x^{+})\leq\Delta(x) because the objective never increases. Since 1−αk≥01-\alpha_{k}\geq 0, induction on (A.10) gives Δ⁡(xk)≤Ek\Delta(x^{k})\leq E_{k}. ∎

The proposition uses only quantities realized in one run, so it holds on every recorded trajectory without assumptions on the local solver beyond returning a block that scores no worse than the current one. Under the best-combination merge, κ\kappa can be replaced by the realized number of colors κk∗\kappa^{*}_{k} (Corollary 1), and, with pairwise factors and all combinations checked, by the effective number of colors κk\kappa_{k} (Proposition 2, Appendix E.9). Appendix E.8 evaluates it on the recorded LLM runs.

A.3. How much private work is worth doing

Section 7 charges at most c>0c>0 for one parallel private step, which lasts as long as its slowest agent, and at most C≥0C\geq 0 for each synchronization: correction construction, certification, message transfer, loading, singleton verification and applying the selected edits. These bounds are uniform, and CC does not grow with HH. With exact corrections, let Tε​(H)T_{\varepsilon}(H) denote the modeled cost of running enough epochs to make the expected gap at most ε\varepsilon. For 0<ε<Δ⁡(x0)0<\varepsilon<\Delta(x^{0}),

(A.11) Kε​(H)≔⌈κμ​q​(H)​log⁡Δ⁡(x0)ε⌉,Tε​(H)≤(c​H+C)​Kε​(H).\begin{gathered}K_{\varepsilon}(H)\coloneqq\left\lceil\frac{\kappa}{\mu q(H)}\log\frac{\Delta(x^{0})}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil,\\ T_{\varepsilon}(H)\leq(cH+C)K_{\varepsilon}(H).\end{gathered}

Indeed, using 1−t≤e−t1-t\leq e^{-t},

𝔼​Δ​(xKε)≤(15)(1−α)Kε​Δ​(x0)≤e−α​Kε​Δ​(x0)​≤(14),(A.11)​ε.\begin{array}[]{rcl}\mathbb{E}\Delta(x^{K_{\varepsilon}})&\overset{\eqref{eq:rate}}{\leq}&(1-\alpha)^{K_{\varepsilon}}\Delta(x^{0})\\ &\leq&e^{-\alpha K_{\varepsilon}}\Delta(x^{0})\overset{\eqref{eq:constants},\eqref{dev:eq:time}}{\leq}\varepsilon.\end{array}

If correction size or evaluation cost grows with the horizon, one must replace CC by that actual bound before optimizing. Token work also grows with the total number of agents’ private steps.

Let ρ≔minb⁡ρb\rho\coloneqq\min_{b}\rho_{b} and λ≔−log⁡(1−ρ)>0\lambda\coloneqq-\log(1-\rho)>0. Dropping the outer ceiling in (A.11) and allowing a real-valued horizon yields the objective

(A.12) J⁡(H)≔c​H+C1−e−λ​H,H>0.J(H)\coloneqq\frac{cH+C}{1-e^{-\lambda H}},\qquad H>0.
Proposition A.3 (A finite useful private-work horizon).

For C>0C>0, JJ has a unique positive minimizer H∗H_{*}, characterized by (20). Over integer H≥1H\geq 1, it suffices to compare the neighboring integers around H∗H_{*}, clamped to one. For C=0C=0, the integer optimum is H=1H=1. These optimize the relaxed bound, not necessarily the ceiled bound or actual runtime.

Proof idea.

The derivative has the sign of a single strictly increasing function. Its unique zero balances the extra cost of one more private step against the additional improvement that step buys.

Proof.

Differentiating (A.12) gives

(A.13) J′​(H)​=(A.12)​c⁡[1−e−λ​H]−λ⁡(c​H+C)​e−λ​H(1−e−λ​H)2.J^{\prime}(H)\overset{\eqref{eq:ratio}}{=}\frac{c[1-e^{-\lambda H}]-\lambda(cH+C)e^{-\lambda H}}{(1-e^{-\lambda H})^{2}}.

Its sign is the sign of ψ⁡(H)=eλ​H−1−λ​H−λ​C/c\psi(H)=e^{\lambda H}-1-\lambda H-\lambda C/c. For C>0C>0, ψ⁡(0)<0\psi(0)<0, ψ′​(H)=λ⁡(eλ​H−1)>0\psi^{\prime}(H)=\lambda(e^{\lambda H}-1)>0 for H>0H>0, and ψ⁡(H)\psi(H) tends to infinity. Hence there is exactly one zero, with JJ decreasing before and increasing after it. This proves both the continuous and integer claims. For C=0C=0, et>1+te^{t}>1+t for t>0t>0 gives J′​(H)>0J^{\prime}(H)>0. ∎

As HH increases, q⁡(H)q(H) approaches one: the analysis interpolates between inexact and exact block minimization. It supplies a batching calculation, not ProxSkip-type communication acceleration.

A.4. Learning the correction

A global objective evaluation can teach the correction if it reveals something reusable. We obtain this property by assuming that the unknown part of the objective has fixed coefficients multiplying known features. Evaluations then give linear equations for those coefficients. Learning them once can help evaluate many later candidates, even as the solution changes.

In the next assumption, G⁡(x)G(x) is the known part of the objective. The vector ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) contains rr known numerical features, and the unknown vector ϑ\vartheta gives their weights. A probe is a feasible candidate evaluated to learn these weights; it need not become the team’s next solution. We call these learning evaluations calibration.

Assumption A.1 (Static identifiable residual).

For a positive integer rr, there are a known function GG, known features ϕ:𝒳→ℝr\phi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{r}, and an unknown fixed vector ϑ∈ℝr\vartheta\in\mathbb{R}^{r} such that

(A.14) F⁡(x)=G⁡(x)+⟨ϑ,ϕ⁡(x)⟩+c0.F(x)=G(x)+\langle\vartheta,\phi(x)\rangle+c_{0}.

The unknown constant c0c_{0} cancels in differences. Known terms and features can be evaluated locally after context loading; their costs are charged. Exact scalar verifier queries are permitted on feasible speculative solutions. Feature changes obey known bounds

(A.15) ‖ϕ⁡(x−b,u)−ϕ⁡(x)‖2≤Λb.\|\phi(x_{-b},u)-\phi(x)\|_{2}\leq\Lambda_{b}.

The representation helps only if rr and the cost of evaluating GG and ϕ\phi are small. The unknown residual here means F−G−c0F-G-c_{0}; the measurement residual introduced next instead means an observed value minus its prediction.

An objective difference gives a linear measurement.

At base xx, query a feasible probe zz and compute

(A.16) a≔ϕ⁡(z)−ϕ⁡(x),y≔F⁡(z)−F⁡(x)−[G⁡(z)−G⁡(x)]=(A.14)​⟨a,ϑ⟩.\begin{gathered}a\coloneqq\phi(z)-\phi(x),\\ y\coloneqq F(z)-F(x)-[G(z)-G(x)]\\ \overset{\eqref{dev:eq:features}}{=}\langle a,\vartheta\rangle.\end{gathered}

Let ϑ^\widehat{\vartheta} denote the current estimate of the unknown weights. Its predicted measurement is ⟨a,ϑ^⟩\langle a,\widehat{\vartheta}\rangle, so y−⟨a,ϑ^⟩y-\langle a,\widehat{\vartheta}\rangle is the prediction error, or residual. For a≠0a\neq 0, the following update moves the estimate to the nearest vector consistent with the observed measurement. The superscript ++ denotes the updated estimate, which is retained for later epochs:

(A.17) ϑ^+≔ϑ^+y−⟨a,ϑ^⟩‖a‖22​a.\widehat{\vartheta}^{+}\coloneqq\widehat{\vartheta}+\frac{y-\langle a,\widehat{\vartheta}\rangle}{\|a\|_{2}^{2}}a.

For intuition, return to the one-bit example and take the known part to be G⁡(u)=L⁡(u)=uG(u)=L(u)=u and the feature to be ϕ⁡(u)=u\phi(u)=u. The unknown coefficient is ϑ=−2\vartheta=-2 and the constant is c0=1c_{0}=1. Evaluating the change from zero to one gives a=1a=1 and y=−2y=-2: the global change is −1-1 and the known local change is +1+1. Starting from an estimate of zero, the update sets it to −2-2. The corrected local objective then prefers one. This example requires only one measurement because it has one unknown coefficient; larger models need enough informative directions.

Learning the two-block example.

The task (A.2) has known part and features

(A.18) G(x)=x1+x2+14(x1−x2)2,ϕ(x)=(x1,x2),ϑ=(−2,−2),c0=2.\begin{gathered}G(x)=x_{1}+x_{2}+\tfrac{1}{4}(x_{1}-x_{2})^{2},\quad\phi(x)=(x_{1},x_{2}),\\ \vartheta=(-2,-2),\qquad c_{0}=2.\end{gathered}

The algorithm knows GG and ϕ\phi, but must learn ϑ\vartheta. Start with ϑ^=(0,0)\widehat{\vartheta}=(0,0) at x=(0,0)x=(0,0). Evaluating the probe z=(1,0)z=(1,0) gives global change −0.75-0.75 and known-part change 1.251.25. Their difference is y=−2y=-2, while a=(1,0)a=(1,0). Update (A.17) therefore sets the first estimated coefficient to −2-2 and leaves the second at zero. The probe is a measurement; it does not itself change the shared solution.

With that estimate, block 1’s corrected candidate now has score −0.75-0.75, so local search can propose it and verification can accept it. After this accepted update, the base is (1,0)(1,0). A probe at (1,1)(1,1) gives global change −1.25-1.25, known-part change 0.750.75, and hence the same unknown coefficient value −2-2 for block 2. Its exact correction is now −2.25-2.25, rather than the value −1.75-1.75 at the original base. The coefficient is static; the complete correction function is not. Known coupling terms must still be recomputed at the current context.

This two-query sequence illustrates coefficient reuse. It is an explanatory sequence; a general rate needs the excitation assumption below.

The update is the established Kaczmarz/sketch-and-project estimator (Strohmer and Vershynin, 2009; Gower and Richtárik, 2015). Ordinary verified edits can supply such measurements too, but they need not explore all parameter directions. We therefore permit deliberate calibration probes that are evaluated without being committed.

Measurements must reveal every unknown direction, not repeatedly test the same one. The next assumption expresses this coverage, often called excitation. Here II is the identity matrix, ⪰\succeq is the positive-semidefinite matrix order, and ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} is the history before epoch kk’s calibration. A larger σ\sigma means a stronger guaranteed coverage of parameter directions.

Assumption A.2 (Exciting calibration).

Conditionally on all past information before calibration, the measurement projector P=a​a⊤/‖a‖22P=aa^{\top}/\|a\|_{2}^{2} satisfies

(A.19) 𝔼⁡[P∣ℋk]⪰σ​I,σ∈(0,1/r].\mathbb{E}[P\mid\mathcal{H}_{k}]\succeq\sigma I,\qquad\sigma\in(0,1/r].

A skipped probe has P=0P=0 and leaves the estimate unchanged; zero-length measurements are skipped. Their probability is included in σ\sigma.

For example, uniformly sampling one of the rr coordinate directions gives 𝔼⁡[P]=I/r\mathbb{E}[P]=I/r, so σ=1/r\sigma=1/r is valid. Taking traces also shows that a single rank-one probe per epoch cannot give σ>1/r\sigma>1/r. Thus the amount and diversity of measurement information matter. This assumption is a property of an implementable probe distribution, not a consequence of successful task edits. The coordinate specialization below instead samples the remaining uncertain coordinates and uses an observable-radius analysis.

From the estimate to private work.

After calibration, replace the unknown vector in the exact correction by its estimate:

(A.20) R^b​(u,x)≔G⁡(x−b,u)−G⁡(x)−[Lb​(u)−Lb​(xb)]+⟨ϑ^+,ϕ⁡(x−b,u)−ϕ⁡(x)⟩.\begin{gathered}\widehat{R}_{b}(u;x)\coloneqq G(x_{-b},u)-G(x)\\ {}-[L_{b}(u)-L_{b}(x_{b})]+\langle\widehat{\vartheta}^{+},\phi(x_{-b},u)-\phi(x)\rangle.\end{gathered}

Substituting into the surrogate makes the implemented local score explicit:

(A.21) f^b​(u,x)​=(4),(A.20)​G​(x−b,u)−G⁡(x)+⟨ϑ^+,ϕ⁡(x−b,u)−ϕ⁡(x)⟩.\begin{gathered}\widehat{f}_{b}(u;x)\overset{\eqref{eq:surrogate},\eqref{eq:learnedcorrection}}{=}G(x_{-b},u)-G(x)\\ {}+\langle\widehat{\vartheta}^{+},\phi(x_{-b},u)-\phi(x)\rangle.\end{gathered}

Thus the implemented method is block descent on the learned global surrogate F^​(x)=G⁡(x)+⟨ϑ^+,ϕ⁡(x)⟩\widehat{F}(x)=G(x)+\langle\widehat{\vartheta}^{+},\phi(x)\rangle. The local objective cancels algebraically; in this representation it supplies a modeling decomposition, not an extra source of optimization power. This exposes the actual computational requirement: after receiving the needed context and coefficients, the agent must evaluate the known terms and features cheaply. The saving comes from this representation and reuse, not from subtracting and adding LbL_{b}. A coefficient vector whose evaluation is as expensive as the verifier would not solve the cost problem.

Then run the same HH-step private solver, verify singleton gains, and merge the best color. Write ϑ^=ϑ^k\widehat{\vartheta}=\widehat{\vartheta}^{k} for the estimate before the calibration of epoch kk and ϑ^+=ϑ^k+1\widehat{\vartheta}^{+}=\widehat{\vartheta}^{k+1} for the estimate after it. With ϑ~≔ϑ^−ϑ\widetilde{\vartheta}\coloneqq\widehat{\vartheta}-\vartheta and ϑ~+≔ϑ^+−ϑ\widetilde{\vartheta}^{+}\coloneqq\widehat{\vartheta}^{+}-\vartheta, the surrogate error is bounded by

(A.22) supu|R^b​(u,x)−Rb​(u,x)|​≤(3),(A.14),(A.15),(A.20)​Λb​‖ϑ~+‖2.\sup_{u}|\widehat{R}_{b}(u;x)-R_{b}(u;x)|\overset{\eqref{eq:correction},\eqref{dev:eq:features},\eqref{dev:eq:featurebound},\eqref{eq:learnedcorrection}}{\leq}\Lambda_{b}\|\widetilde{\vartheta}^{+}\|_{2}.

The unknown error norm is only used in analysis. Section A.5 supplies an observable certificate for coordinate residuals.

Lemma A.4 (Learning contracts a persistent error).

Under Assumptions A.1 and A.2, let η≔1−σ<1\eta\coloneqq\sqrt{1-\sigma}<1. Then

(A.23) 𝔼⁡[‖ϑ~+‖2∣ℋk]≤η​‖ϑ~‖2.\mathbb{E}[\|\widetilde{\vartheta}^{+}\|_{2}\mid\mathcal{H}_{k}]\leq\eta\|\widetilde{\vartheta}\|_{2}.
Proof idea.

The update removes precisely the component of coefficient error along the measured direction. The excitation assumption ensures that, on average, every direction loses a definite fraction of its squared error.

Proof.

An active update is an orthogonal projection of the error:

(A.24) ϑ~+​=(A.16),(A.17)​(I−P)​ϑ~,‖ϑ~+‖22​=(A.16),(A.17)​‖ϑ~‖22−ϑ~⊤​P​ϑ~.\begin{gathered}\widetilde{\vartheta}^{+}\overset{\eqref{dev:eq:measurement},\eqref{dev:eq:project}}{=}(I-P)\widetilde{\vartheta},\\ \|\widetilde{\vartheta}^{+}\|_{2}^{2}\overset{\eqref{dev:eq:measurement},\eqref{dev:eq:project}}{=}\|\widetilde{\vartheta}\|_{2}^{2}-\widetilde{\vartheta}^{\top}P\widetilde{\vartheta}.\end{gathered}

The same identities hold for a skipped update with P=0P=0. Conditioning and applying the excitation bound gives

(A.25) 𝔼⁡[‖ϑ~+‖22∣ℋk]​≤(A.24),(A.19)​(1−σ)​‖ϑ~‖22.\mathbb{E}[\|\widetilde{\vartheta}^{+}\|_{2}^{2}\mid\mathcal{H}_{k}]\overset{\eqref{eq:pythagoras},\eqref{dev:eq:excitation}}{\leq}(1-\sigma)\|\widetilde{\vartheta}\|_{2}^{2}.

Jensen’s inequality for the square root proves (A.23). Since ϑ\vartheta is fixed, committing a new solution does not change the parameter error. This persistence is the crucial benefit of the representation. ∎

We can now track both processes together. Searching with an inaccurate correction leaves an additional task-error term proportional to the parameter error; calibration reduces that parameter error. Weighting the two errors appropriately gives one quantity that decreases geometrically. This quantity is an analysis tool: it contains the unknown optimum and unknown true weights, so the algorithm cannot use it as a stopping test.

What is coupled to what?

The potential 𝒱k\mathcal{V}_{k} below adds ω\omega times the coefficient error ‖ϑ^k−ϑ‖2\|\widehat{\vartheta}^{k}-\vartheta\|_{2} to the task gap. Calibration reduces its conditional expectation by a factor η<1\eta<1. Meanwhile, optimization reduces task error by a factor 1−α1-\alpha, but adds a penalty proportional to the coefficient error remaining after calibration. The proof combines these two statements. The coefficient β\beta converts parameter error into objective-error units; the weight ω\omega makes their weighted sum decrease. A potential is simply this weighted quantity used to track the analysis, not an additional objective that an agent minimizes.

Theorem A.5 (A joint task–correction contraction).

Assume known graph structure, Assumption 2 for every learned surrogate, Assumption 3, and Assumptions A.1–A.2. Set

(A.26) α≔μq(H)/κ,β≔κ−1∑b(1+qb(H))Λb>0,ω≔2β/(1−η),τ≔min{α,(1−η)/2},𝒱k≔Δ⁡(xk)+ω​‖ϑ^k−ϑ‖2.\begin{gathered}\alpha\coloneqq\mu q(H)/\kappa,\quad\beta\coloneqq\kappa^{-1}\sum_{b}(1+q_{b}(H))\Lambda_{b}>0,\\ \omega\coloneqq 2\beta/(1-\eta),\quad\tau\coloneqq\min\{\alpha,(1-\eta)/2\},\\ \mathcal{V}_{k}\coloneqq\Delta(x^{k})+\omega\|\widehat{\vartheta}^{k}-\vartheta\|_{2}.\end{gathered}

With deterministic initialization,

(A.27) 𝔼​𝒱K≤(1−τ)K​𝒱0.\mathbb{E}\mathcal{V}_{K}\leq(1-\tau)^{K}\mathcal{V}_{0}.

Thus solution error and correction error vanish together; no externally supplied shrinking-error schedule is needed.

Proof idea.

Optimization contracts the task error but pays a penalty proportional to the remaining coefficient error. Calibration contracts that coefficient error. The weight ω\omega is chosen so that the latter decrease pays for the former penalty.

Proof.

Condition first on the calibration outcome. The drift bound (A.5) applies with the current errors bounded by (A.22). Averaging over calibration yields

(A.28) 𝔼⁡[Δ⁡(xk+1)∣ℋk]≤(A.5),(A.22),(A.26)​(1−α)​Δ​(xk)+β​𝔼​[‖ϑ~+‖2∣ℋk].\begin{gathered}\mathbb{E}[\Delta(x^{k+1})\mid\mathcal{H}_{k}]\\ \overset{\eqref{eq:drift},\eqref{eq:learnederror},\eqref{dev:eq:jointconstants}}{\leq}(1-\alpha)\Delta(x^{k})+\beta\mathbb{E}[\|\widetilde{\vartheta}^{+}\|_{2}\mid\mathcal{H}_{k}].\end{gathered}

Adding the weighted learning error gives

(A.29) 𝔼⁡[𝒱k+1∣ℋk]≤(A.28),(A.23)(1−α)​Δ​(xk)+(β+ω)​η​‖ϑ~‖2≤(A.26)(1−τ)​𝒱k.\begin{gathered}\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{V}_{k+1}\mid\mathcal{H}_{k}]\\ \begin{array}[]{c@{\;}l}\overset{\eqref{eq:coupled},\eqref{eq:learncontract}}{\leq}&(1-\alpha)\Delta(x^{k})+(\beta+\omega)\eta\|\widetilde{\vartheta}\|_{2}\\ \overset{\eqref{dev:eq:jointconstants}}{\leq}&(1-\tau)\mathcal{V}_{k}.\end{array}\end{gathered}

For the second step, τ≤α\tau\leq\alpha and (β+ω)​η≤ω⁡[1−(1−η)/2](\beta+\omega)\eta\leq\omega[1-(1-\eta)/2]; the latter follows because the difference equals β⁡(1−η)≥0\beta(1-\eta)\geq 0. Taking expectations and induction prove (A.27). ∎

In this theorem, Lemma 1 is applied epoch by epoch, after conditioning on the calibration result. Its error bound may therefore change from epoch to epoch; no fixed nonzero error floor is imposed. The rate τ\tau is controlled by the slower of two processes: optimizing the solution with the current correction, and identifying the correction itself. The method retains an estimate of fixed coefficients, not a permanently valid table of candidate values: after xx changes, known features and coupling terms must still be evaluated at the new context. This is the precise sense in which the correction is reusable.

Can already-paid verification teach the correction?

Yes. Every proposal verified in line 6 of Algorithm 1, including a rejected one, supplies a measurement at the common base. With zb=(x−b,Ub)z_{b}=(x_{-b},U_{b}), define

(A.30) ab≔ϕ⁡(zb)−ϕ⁡(x),yb≔F⁡(zb)−F⁡(x)−[G⁡(zb)−G⁡(x)]​=(A.14)​⟨ab,ϑ⟩.\begin{gathered}a_{b}\coloneqq\phi(z_{b})-\phi(x),\\ y_{b}\coloneqq F(z_{b})-F(x)-[G(z_{b})-G(x)]\overset{\eqref{dev:eq:features}}{=}\langle a_{b},\vartheta\rangle.\end{gathered}

One can apply (A.17) to these measurements after all proposals and merge decisions have been fixed, retaining the resulting estimate for the next epoch. Each equation must use the base at which its two objective values were measured. Reuse needs no additional verifier call; feature evaluation, projection work, and communicating the updated estimate still cost work.

Proposition A.6 (Safe reuse of proposal measurements).

Under the hypotheses of Theorem A.5, keep its deliberate calibration and add any finite sequence of exact projection updates from the already-evaluated proposals, after the current search and merge decision. The bound (A.27) remains valid for the estimate after these extra updates. No excitation or independence assumption is needed for the extra measurements.

Proof idea.

Extra projections cannot increase parameter error. They do not change the proposals used to prove this epoch’s task-error bound.

Proof.

Let ϑ~+\widetilde{\vartheta}^{+} be the error just after deliberate calibration, and let ϑ~next\widetilde{\vartheta}^{\rm next} be its value after all proposal measurements have been processed. Every nonzero measurement gives an orthogonal projection; a zero measurement is skipped. Repeated use of the pathwise identity (A.24) gives

(A.31) ‖ϑ~next‖2​≤(A.24)​‖ϑ~+‖2.\|\widetilde{\vartheta}^{\rm next}\|_{2}\overset{\eqref{eq:pythagoras}}{\leq}\|\widetilde{\vartheta}^{+}\|_{2}.

The task update still obeys (A.28). Consequently

𝔼⁡[𝒱k+1∣ℋk]≤(A.28),(A.31),(A.23)(1−α)​Δ​(xk)+(β+ω)​η​‖ϑ~‖2≤(A.26)(1−τ)​𝒱k.\begin{gathered}\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{V}_{k+1}\mid\mathcal{H}_{k}]\\ \begin{array}[]{c@{\;}l}\overset{\eqref{eq:coupled},\eqref{eq:reuse-norm},\eqref{eq:learncontract}}{\leq}&(1-\alpha)\Delta(x^{k})+(\beta+\omega)\eta\|\widetilde{\vartheta}\|_{2}\\ \overset{\eqref{dev:eq:jointconstants}}{\leq}&(1-\tau)\mathcal{V}_{k}.\end{array}\end{gathered}

Induction proves the claim. The next epoch’s hypotheses must continue to hold for the augmented history, as required by their uniform conditional formulation. ∎

This extension justifies learning from verification, but does not justify removing deliberate calibration: proposals can all have zero measurement vectors or fail to explore an unknown direction.

The joint theorem shows that learning and optimization can converge together. Yet its estimation error involves the unknown true coefficients, so the algorithm cannot read that error from its current state. Nor does a rate in epochs alone reveal the price of the measurements. A more concrete specialization lets us address both issues.

A.5. Certifying and paying for learning

For binary blocks with unknown individual-bit penalties, each targeted objective evaluation identifies one coefficient exactly. This gives both a computable bound on the remaining correction error and a finite total number of learning queries. We now derive those guarantees. Unlike the preceding parameter-error norm, the remaining uncertainty can be tracked without knowing the true weights. For this specialization, assume 𝒳b={0,1}db\mathcal{X}_{b}=\{0,1\}^{d_{b}} with positive integer dbd_{b}. Thus every one-bit calibration probe is feasible; a constrained subset of the binary cube need not have this property. Let Ψ\Psi be a known function describing interactions between blocks. Assume all remaining unknown requirements are linear penalties on individual bits:

(A.32) F⁡(x)=∑bLb​(xb)+Ψ⁡(x)+∑b⟨ϑb,xb⟩+c0.F(x)=\sum_{b}L_{b}(x_{b})+\Psi(x)+\sum_{b}\langle\vartheta_{b},x_{b}\rangle+c_{0}.

The unknown c0c_{0} cancels in differences. Assume known coordinate bounds |ϑb​j−ϑ^b​j0|≤Mb​j|\vartheta_{bj}-\widehat{\vartheta}^{0}_{bj}|\leq M_{bj}. A probe flips bit jj of block bb at the current base, producing zz and s=zb​j−xb​j∈{−1,1}s=z_{bj}-x_{bj}\in\{-1,1\}. Its residual is

(A.33) y≔F⁡(z)−F⁡(x)−[Lb​(zb)−Lb​(xb)]−[Ψ⁡(z)−Ψ⁡(x)]​=(A.32)​s​ϑb​j,ϑ^b​j+≔ϑ^b​j+(y−s​ϑ^b​j)/s.\begin{gathered}y\coloneqq F(z)-F(x)-[L_{b}(z_{b})-L_{b}(x_{b})]\\ {}-[\Psi(z)-\Psi(x)]\overset{\eqref{dev:eq:coordinate-model}}{=}s\vartheta_{bj},\\ \widehat{\vartheta}_{bj}^{+}\coloneqq\widehat{\vartheta}_{bj}+(y-s\widehat{\vartheta}_{bj})/s.\end{gathered}

Write γ≔p/dmax\gamma\coloneqq p/d_{\max}. The above calibration satisfies

Each successful probe removes one previously unmeasured coefficient from the uncertainty sum. Bounding the expected removed uncertainty gives contraction; counting distinct coefficients gives the finite query budget.

Every calibration identifies a previously unobserved coefficient, so its count is at most dtotd_{\rm tot}. At most m​pmp queries occur in expectation per epoch, proving both bounds. ∎
